keyed

a key that stays unique through the pipeline

keyed attaches a primary key to a data frame read from a flat file, such as a CSV or Excel export, and stops a dplyr pipeline at the step that makes the key non-unique.

The key is stored with the data frame as metadata, and keyed’s methods for the dplyr verbs carry it from step to step. Whenever a step changes the key values or the number of rows, the key is checked for uniqueness with vctrs, and a step that creates duplicates stops with an error. A database enforces this through its schema, while a CSV accepts whatever it is given. You can then correct the data, or remove the key with unkey() when the step is meant to repeat key values. keyed supports:

  • Checks at chosen points. lock_unique(), lock_no_na(), lock_complete(), lock_coverage() and lock_nrow() test a condition inside a pipeline and warn when it fails, or stop with .strict = TRUE.
  • Previewing a join. diagnose_join() reports whether a join is one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many before it runs, with the more detailed report of joinspy when that package is installed.
  • Tracking rows without a natural key. add_id() gives each row an identifier that stays with it through filters and joins, and compare_ids() lists the rows a step lost.
  • Seeing what a step changed. A data frame marked with watch() is saved before each dplyr verb, and check_drift() reports the rows removed, added and modified since then, column by column.

Installation 

install.packages("keyed")

Development version:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/keyed")

Usage

  1. Declare the key columns with key().
  2. Transform the data with dplyr as usual. The key is checked whenever a step changes the key values or the number of rows.
  3. Add checks such as lock_no_na() where the pipeline relies on a condition.

key() takes a data frame and one or more unquoted column names. It checks that their combined values are unique and warns if they are not.

library(keyed)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

customers <- data.frame(
  customer_id = c(1, 2, 3),
  name = c("Ann", "Bob", "Cy")
)
customers <- key(customers, customer_id)
customers
#> # A keyed tibble: 3 x 2
#> # Key:            customer_id
#>   customer_id name 
#>         <dbl> <chr>
#> 1           1 Ann  
#> 2           2 Bob  
#> 3           3 Cy

A filter keeps the key, since removing rows cannot create duplicates. A join that repeats customers stops with an error:

orders <- data.frame(order_id = 1:5, customer_id = c(1, 1, 2, 3, 3))

customers |> filter(customer_id > 1) |> has_key()
#> [1] TRUE
left_join(customers, orders, by = "customer_id")
#> Error in `dplyr_reconstruct_dispatch()`:
#> ! Key is no longer unique after transformation.
#> ℹ Use `unkey()` first if you intend to break uniqueness.

Customers 1 and 3 have two orders each, so the joined table has five rows and customer_id is no longer unique. diagnose_join(customers, orders, by = "customer_id") shows this before the join runs. To keep the five rows, drop the key first with unkey().

Checks at chosen points

A lock tests one condition and returns the data unchanged, so it sits inside a pipeline:

emails <- data.frame(id = 1:3, email = c("a@x.org", NA, "c@x.org"))
checked <- emails |> lock_unique(id) |> lock_no_na(email)
#> Warning: No-NA assumption violated.
#> ℹ Columns with NA values: email (1 NA)

lock_complete() checks every column for missing values, lock_coverage() sets a minimum share of non-missing values, and lock_nrow() a range of row counts. Each one warns by default and stops with .strict = TRUE.

Tracking rows and changes

add_id() adds a column of row identifiers (UUIDs when the uuid package is installed), and compare_ids() returns the identifiers lost, gained and kept between two versions of a table:

tracked <- add_id(customers)
kept <- tracked |> filter(name != "Bob")
compare_ids(tracked, kept)

For values, diff() aligns two versions of a keyed table by the key and counts the rows removed, added and modified, with the changes per column:

old <- key(data.frame(id = 1:3, x = c("a", "b", "c")), id)
new <- data.frame(id = 2:4, x = c("B", "c", "d"))
diff(old, new)
#> 
#> ── Value Diff
#> Key: id
#> 
#> ! Removed: 1 row(s)
#> ℹ Added: 1 row(s)
#> ! Modified: 1 row(s)
#> x: 1 change(s)
#> Unchanged: 1 row(s)

watch() makes this automatic: each dplyr verb on a watched table first saves a snapshot in memory, and check_drift() compares the result with it. unwatch() stops the snapshots and clear_all_snapshots() frees the memory.

keyed or pointblank / validate?

keyed pointblank, validate
Setup A key declared inline A schema or rule set written beforehand
Checks during dplyr steps Yes, on every verb that changes the key or row count No
Scope Keys, locks, row identifiers, drift Full validation rule sets and reports
Suited to Interactive work with CSV and Excel files Batch validation and reporting

For a schema that is enforced on every write, a database such as SQLite or DuckDB is the tool, and pointblank or validate produce full validation reports. keyed holds a few assumptions about a flat file during interactive work, without a database or a rule set.
